Then there was a bit of a time where things did slow down when it was coming from the frontier. We had a lot of scaffolding for the agents and we were very particular about how these models ran. It was much more like a workflow. What this allowed us to do was get really high quality and also very accurate, but also just very consistent, which is very important for us in the regulatory space, outputs. Then one fortuitous thing as part of doing this, because we wanted to have some way to regression test this big system, we ended up with a really large set of evaluation samples. We had tens of thousands actually of hand-labeled examples by experts. We were able to just take this benchmark set and just immediately run on top of it with some of these more agentic approaches. Then from that we left with basically a set of specs about what this platform needed to be able to do to enable two things. One, deliver agentic experiences to our clients. Then also it needed to be amenable to having AIs like co-developers alongside of our own development team. That's what we've been executing against ever since then. I think you hit on a key point, Scott, which is the eval side of the fence that you were talking about before. I've seen across the board as model versions change underneath the covers, you get different answers. You get skew in terms of the accuracy of information that comes back.
